cues.text: A Small Church Outside the City
In the twelfth century, the church of Santa Maria in Vado stood on what was then the edge of Ferrara.
It was a modest chapel in the care of the Canons Regular Portuensi and, since 1135, under the custody of the local bishop.
Nothing about its size or setting would have suggested it was destined to become one of the most visited Eucharistic shrines in Italy.
Blood Upon the Vault

On Easter Sunday, March 28, 1171, tradition holds, the church's prior, Father Pietro da Verona, was celebrating Solemn Mass with three fellow canons when he reached the moment of breaking the consecrated host.
At that instant, the account relates, blood sprayed forth from the host itself, splattering the small stone vault above the altar with droplets of deep red.

Contemporary testimonies, tradition says, describe both the celebrant's fear and the wonder of the congregation crowded into the tiny church, some of whom reported seeing the figure of an infant within the reddened host.
Examined by Bishop and Archbishop
Word reached Bishop Amato of Ferrara and Archbishop Gerard of Ravenna.
Both are said to have come in person to examine the stained vault.
They later attested to having personally seen what they called "the Blood which we saw redden the ceiling."
Their episcopal testimony, distinct from a later devotional retelling, is part of what distinguishes Ferrara's account from many contemporaries.
Word of the sign spread quickly, and the small church soon became a site of regular pilgrimage from across the region.
A Shrine Built to Last
In 1595, the stained portion of the vault was enclosed within its own small shrine chapel, still visible today within the larger Basilica of Santa Maria in Vado as it was later rebuilt and expanded.
An inscription placed at the site records the tradition in plain terms: the blood, it says, "leaping forth in the midst of the priest's hands by a miracle, stuck to the upper part of this apse."
Across the centuries, the shrine has drawn a notable line of pilgrims, including several popes.
Tradition holds that Pope St. John Paul II visited in 1990, continuing a pattern of papal attention reaching back to Pope Alexander III in the twelfth century.
Legacy
We recognize in the account of Ferrara something the Church has returned to again and again across the centuries of Eucharistic devotion.
It was not a doubt confronted privately, as at Rome or Scetis, but a public sign witnessed by an entire congregation.
The bishops responsible for it then examined that sign, soberly and deliberately.
That combination has helped the tradition endure for over eight centuries with unusual consistency.

The stains remain visible today for any pilgrim willing to climb to the small vault above the altar, a quiet and enduring witness, in the words carved beside them, to wonder, adore, and give thanks to God.
